lesson.title: Free Exchange: Understanding Open Systems
lesson.summary: An open system can exchange both matter and energy with its surroundings, making it the least contained but also the most common kind of system encountered in everyday chemistry.
lesson.body:
An open system is one whose boundary allows both matter, meaning actual physical substance such as atoms or molecules, and energy, such as heat, to cross freely between the system and its surroundings.

A pot of water boiling on a stove with no lid is a clear example. Heat energy flows in continuously from the burner, crossing the boundary as an energy transfer. At the same time, as the water boils, steam escapes upward into the air: actual matter, in the form of water vapor, leaves the system and does not come back. Because both channels are open at once, the system is genuinely losing mass, the water level visibly drops as boiling continues, while also constantly exchanging energy with the surrounding air and burner.

Living organisms are open systems for the same reason: they take in matter such as food, water, and oxygen, release matter such as carbon dioxide and waste, and exchange thermal energy with their environment the entire time, all simultaneously. Even a simple open beaker in a lab, containing a reaction that releases gas, qualifies as an open system, since the gas is free to escape into the room while heat also passes through the glass.

Tracking energy changes alone is not enough to fully describe what is happening in an open system, since mass leaving or entering the system carries its own share of energy along with it, which makes open systems the hardest of the three categories to analyze completely. They are also, importantly, the realistic default: almost every everyday chemical process, cooking a meal, a person breathing, an uncapped reaction flask, is technically an open system unless someone deliberately does something to seal it off, which is exactly what turns it into a closed system instead.
